cards.title: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3

depth.text: Safari can turn **bright websites** dark even when their creators never added **dark mode**

**Almost 40%** of page loads come from users in dark mode, but **only 10%** support it. In Safari 27.3 beta, it estimates whether a page is mostly light or dark, transforms light pages, and leaves sites that declare dark-mode support alone. JavaScript still gets the **original authored colors**, so websites can’t detect the change.
data: web page loads from users in dark mode

cards.camps: Two camps: dark-mode users welcome browsers darkening bright sites; people with astigmatism say white-on-black is hard to read and want dark sites turned light.

depth.text: someone explains how **PostgreSQL works inside**, from **query processing** to storage

It has chapters on **query processing**, the **buffer manager**, and write-ahead logging, and covers versions **19-beta and earlier** except the new buffer page lock mechanism. One commenter says HOT only kicks in when no indexed column changes and the new tuple fits on the same page.

The latest Jepsen report on particledb triggered a new found interest in the SSI implementation in postgres. If you are just skimming this doc, The HoT update path is the section I would jump to. Chapter 12 (full-text search) quietly changed under this book in Postgres 18: FTS now reads its dictionaries and config through the cluster's default collation provider instead of always libc, so clusters on ICU or the new builtin PG_UNICODE_FAST can see different behavior in FTS and pg_trgm — the release notes explicitly tell you to reindex those indexes after pg_upgrade. cards.title: C++26 Disapproved

depth.text: C++’s next standard **hit a wall** after national bodies voted down its draft over **Contracts**

The **C++26 DIS** missed the required **two-thirds majority** after a **twelve-week voting period**; some national bodies said Contracts was not ready. Every available path forward would delay the next standard.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see Contracts as useful for verification and narrowing C++’s safety gap; others say they add little or worsen the language’s complexity.

comments.text: As someone who writes high-reliability C++ but is completely outside the standards process, I see the issues with C++ Contracts. It isn’t clear that it solves a problem that anyone has in real codebases, especially after C++20 concepts. If you were already writing high-reliability C++ then the benefits are difficult to quantify. If you weren’t writing high-reliability C++ then it saves you almost…

While I can understand that C++ contracts were met with controversy, contract annotations scoped at analysis time that can be verified by external tools, such as static analyzers, model checkers, or automatic theorem provers, are incredibly useful. I put together an alternative function contract and invariant mechanism in C using CBMC and custom macros that effectively allows me to perform formal…

I get why some folks would like to see contracts in the language, but C++ is also buckling due to the shear complexity that's getting tacked on to it. I'd rather see more proposals such as C++26's "erroneous behavior" that attempts to reign in the language's shortcomings.

This article makes it sound the options are normally approval, rejection and abstention, but that this time round a fourth option, "disapproval", was reached. It that the case, or are they just trying to say that people rejected it?
Personally I'd like to see C++ chill out on new features and maybe sort out the shitshow that is char8_t and std::filesystem.

depth.text: people in Japan turned **everyday awkward moments** into **mundane Halloween costumes** that need explaining

The tradition began in **2014** with adults at Daily Portal Z who wanted to join Halloween but felt too embarrassed for witch or zombie costumes. This year's examples include someone about to ask if it’s okay to push their seat back and a person who thought the muddler was a straw.

comments.text: The last one refilling detergent is a parody of The Milkmaid by Johannes Vermeer; everyone has seen it on textbooks and it has become a meme template on Japanese Twitter in recent years. 1: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Milkmaid_(Vermeer)

Some of these are very humorous because of the cultural disconnect (as an American, I have never experienced somebody asking to put their seat back). "An expert on a very niche subject" made me laugh out loud the hardest, because it's the one that's most "just a guy", and yet it's also exactly how it's described.
These are masterpieces in my opinion. It’s difficult to get the vibe exactly right when you’re working with so little. Yes, a thousand times yes you can put your seat back you gentle soul.

They are more like "situational haikus", or the transposition to practical humor of the concept of haiku.

cards.title: Gitbook Breached

depth.text: GitBook says an **AI-agent attack** accessed credentials, taking **services offline** and prompting **customer token resets**

The attacker gained unauthorized access to **some infrastructure credentials at 19:00 CET, November 2**; GitBook says it detected the attack immediately. The company took the app and authenticated docs offline, replaced credentials and secrets, and invalidated customer API tokens. Data that **may have been accessed** includes Git Sync secrets, third-party API tokens, and visitor questions to **GitBook Assistant**.

cards.camps: Two camps: GitBook describes a sophisticated attack using AI agents; skeptics say the wording is vague and question whether AI agents were really involved.

comments.text: GitBook’s CTO here We have been dealing with a security attack since yesterday. Our team has been all hands on deck since the start, and we took a large portion of our services offline to prioritize user security. Our service is progressively coming back online (most of it already is), and we are actively monitoring the situation. We’ll continue to actively keep our users updated through emails…

> sophisticated, highly targeted attack I love the way all incident reports tell you the attack was sophisticated and highly targeted, as if those words actually mean anything. Nobody wants to admit they were DDOSed by a script kiddie just randomly trying exploits. The subtext is: well, we expected hackers; just not really good ones.
Good that they rotated all the tokens themselves instead of just telling users to do it, seen too many incidents where that step gets skipped.

glossary.payload capacity: The heaviest thing a robot can carry while doing its job.
glossary.fiducial tags: Markers a robot can spot with its camera to recognize a place or object.
glossary.inverse kinematics: Working out how a robot's joints need to move to put its hand at a chosen spot.
glossary.color-scheme: A page setting that tells browsers whether the page supports light mode, dark mode, or both.
glossary.CSS: Cascading Style Sheets: rules that control how a web page looks.
glossary.HTML: HyperText Markup Language: code that tells a browser what content a web page has.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.canvas: A webpage area where code can draw pictures or other visuals.
glossary.contrast ratio: A number comparing how different text and background colors look, used to judge readability.
glossary.WCAG: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: recommendations for making web content easier for people with disabilities to use.
glossary.fingerprinting: Using clues from a device and browser to recognize them without relying on a saved cookie.
glossary.off-balance-sheet debt: Money a company is committed to pay that is not listed among its usual debts.
glossary.RPO: Remaining Performance Obligations: money customers have committed to pay for work the company still has to deliver.
glossary.CapEx: Capital expenditures: money a company spends on long-lasting things it needs, like buildings and equipment.
glossary.AGI: Artificial General Intelligence: a hypothetical AI that could handle many kinds of tasks, not just one narrow job.
glossary.inference: When an AI uses what it learned to answer or act, instead of being trained.
glossary.generative model: A program that learns patterns in examples so it can make new examples like them.
glossary.PCA: Principal component analysis: a way to simplify data by keeping its biggest patterns.
glossary.probabilistic PCA: A version of PCA that represents patterns with probabilities, not just fixed values.
glossary.variational autoencoder: A model that learns to make new examples by compressing examples and then recreating them.
glossary.diffusion model: An image-making AI that starts with visual noise and gradually turns it into a picture.
glossary.normalising flow: A model that makes new examples by changing random inputs through steps that can be undone.
glossary.autoregressive factorisation: A way to describe a sequence by predicting each next piece from the pieces before it.
glossary.GAN: Generative adversarial network: a setup where one AI makes examples and another tries to spot fakes.
glossary.Wasserstein GAN: A kind of GAN that judges how different made-up examples are from real ones.
glossary.energy-based model: A model that scores possible examples, with lower scores meaning a better fit.
glossary.linear algebra: A kind of math used to describe how shapes move and turn.
glossary.Algo fatigue: Feeling tired of recommendation feeds deciding what you should watch or read.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.sideloadable: An app you install on a device yourself, instead of getting it through the device's usual app store.
glossary.BrightScript/SceneGraph: Roku's language and app-building tools for making apps that run on Roku devices.
glossary.vibe coding: Making software by telling an AI what you want and letting it write the code, often without closely checking how it works.
glossary.HOT: Heap Only Tuple: a way to update a database row without changing its lookup lists, when no searched column changes and the new row stays on the same page.
glossary.tuple: A single row of data in a database.
glossary.WAL: Write-ahead log: a record of changes the database saves so it can recover or copy them.
glossary.TOAST: The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique: a PostgreSQL feature for storing very large values separately from the main row.
glossary.MVCC: Multi-Version Concurrency Control: a way to keep different copies of a row so people can use the database at the same time.
glossary.DIS: The penultimate stage in the ISO standard process; the C++26 draft failed to get enough votes at this stage.
glossary.WG21: C++ Standardization Committee: the group that discusses and votes on proposed changes to C++.
glossary.NB: National Body: a country-level group that votes on proposed ISO standards.
glossary.Contracts: A way to write expectations about what a function should receive or do, so they can be checked.
glossary.formal methods: Ways to check software against precise rules, rather than relying only on trying it out.
glossary.multi-WAN: A setup that can use more than one internet connection.
glossary.uplink: A connection from a device out to the internet or another network.
glossary.dynamic routing: A network automatically picks a path for information based on which routes are available.
glossary.failover: A backup system taking over automatically when the main one stops working.
glossary.load balancing: Spreading traffic across connections so one connection does not have to handle it all.
glossary.firewall rules: Settings that decide which network connections are allowed in or out.
glossary.VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
glossary.Jimi Halloween: A Japanese Halloween tradition where people dress as mundane everyday situations.
glossary.AI agents: Computer programs that can carry out tasks, rather than only answer a question.
glossary.API token: A secret code that lets another app or person access a service.
glossary.credentials: The username and password that let someone sign in to an account.
glossary.Git Sync: A way to keep GitBook pages and a Git project updated together.
glossary.MCP server: Model Context Protocol server: a computer that lets an AI connect to outside tools or information.
glossary.post mortem: A report written after an incident to explain what happened and what should change.
glossary.teleprompter: A screen that shows someone the words they’re meant to say while speaking.
glossary.IrDA: Infrared Data Association: a group whose name is used for rules that let nearby devices send information with infrared light.
